content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
This paper presents a singing voice synthesis method based on a score-based generative models using stochastic differential equation. It adapted the existing model to the singing voice generation and the proposed method achieve much better qualities. 

Strength: the results are qualitatively impressive, the ablation study is good.
Weakness: the novelty of the paper is limited. It's an application of an off-the-shelf method. There's large amount of equations which mainly explains the existing method and seem unnecessary.
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score: The paper lacks novelty and is an application of existing method.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper describes an end-to-end approach for singing voice synthesis and trains a model on the PopCS dataset of phoneme-aligned a cappella songs. The method consists in first predicting an approximate mel spectrogram from the music score with lyrics; this spectrogram is then used to condition a diffusion based model on mel-spectrograms or on waveform. In the case where the model outputs a melspectrogram, an additional vocoder step (like Hifi-GAN) is required.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

The whole approach is relevant for the problem considered and the examples shown in the accompanying website are highly convincing.
The proposed method seems on par with other models like DiffSinger. The method can be trained end-to-end despite having many components. The ablation study is interesting and shows the superiority of the end-to-end approach over the mel-spectrogram + Hifi-GAN pipeline.

Weaknesses:
It would be interesting to see how stochastic can be the output, as there are many different interpretations for the same music score. In this particular case, it seems that almost all the work is done by the decoder. Providing different outputs could help notice how information not present in the score is added (like breathing).
Maybe adding the output M' on the website could be enlightening to really distinguish the role of the decoder from the role of the denoiser.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
In my opinion, this paper is an adaptation of Popov et al. 2021 (speech synthesis) to the SVS task. The conditioning method (using the M term in Eq. 3) is directly inherited from this paper and this could be stated more clearly.

Adding a figure in order to describe the different architectures in appendix could help, as Sect. 3.5 is quite dense.

The structure and the writing of the paper are surprising at times (Broad related work section lies between model presentation and results, inference section between training and end-to-end training sections) and many now-standard terms are not used (the algorithm described in Sect. 3.3 is the Predictor-Corrector sampling from Song et al.).
The Fokker-Planck equation is not necessary to obtain (5).

The distinction between the different sampling of RealSinger could be made clearer (RealSinger + HifiGAN vs RealSinger E2E) from the beginning. More importantly, the end-to-end method seems to be the top performing one, it could have been interesting to focus on this one, and leave the other one as

Question:
- Is the pre-trained Hifi-GAN trained on this singing voice dataset? 
- log mel spectrograms? 
- Is the mel score predictor part essential?

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper presents a new diffusion-based singing voice synthesis method which results in high-quality singing voice with subjective listening scores close to real singing.
The method relies on a diffusion setup conditioned on encoded musical score and a regressed mel spectrogram in addition to the time-step embedding. The architecture presented allows diffusion of either mel spectrogram or raw waveform. The authors follow the variance preserving SDE formulation of mel spectrogram diffusion and variance exploding SDE for raw waveform.
The authors compare their method against recent SVS systems and show that mean opinion scores are close to real audio.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 
- The results are very convincing. The audio samples shared show that the method is indeed capable of generating realistic singing.
- The presented approach is novel for singing voice synthesis. Compared to DiffSinger which was the first work to apply diffusion to singing voice synthesis, this work does not rely on a shallow diffusion mechanism which involves a more complex setup where a time step regressor needs to be trained to figure out where in the diffusion process a noisy regressed mel spectrogram lies. This approach is cleaner in that it is a pure conditional diffusion model.
- Another strong point is that the authors demonstrate the performance on end-to-end synthesis, which does away with the need to train a separate vocoder.

Weaknesses:
- There are quite a few details missing in the paper. These details are important for the listener to judge the importance and significance of the work. For example: PopCS dataset contains very detailed annotations. It is not made very clear whether the authors use the quantized score or the fine-grained mel-spectrogram aligned score. My guess is that given the quality of the samples, the pitch sequence is the fundamental frequency contour instead of quantized MIDI notes. If not, then the results are even more impressive. Similarly, it's not clear whether the note durations are in quantized form like quarter note, eighth note, etc. Since phoneme duration is given, my guess is that this is also time-algined with the mel-spectrogram. In my opinion, this setup make the task of SVS much simpler since no alignment needs to be learned.
- In addition to task-related details, there are also a lot of key details missing for reproducing the work. These will be discussed in the next section.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper writing is mostly clear. There are a few typos and phrasing issues but nothing major is wrong.

As mentioned above, I find the paper to be novel as there is no existing work in singing voice synthesis which uses a full diffusion setup. There is an audio denoising paper called Universe at Neurips 2022 which uses a similar setup but there are enough differences in both the task and the model setup.

I have some concerns about reproducibility of the work. There are many small but key details missing in the paper which would make reproducing the work very difficult. For example, it is not clear if the authors use fixed length for mel spectrogram/audio during training. It's also unclear if there is any kind of normalization applied to the mel spectrogram. Typically for diffusion models, data is normalized. Mel spectrograms by default lie way outside -1,1 range so they are normalized in most settings.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I am impressed by the quality of the results generated. However I am taking them with a grain of salt as the authors do not adequately explain exactly what conditioning variables are used. However, Diffsinger, the competing approach also uses strong conditioning variables and the results in this work are superior to that. The paper could use some more proofreading but technically it is fine. With this in mind, I am giving the paper an accept rating.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a new method for singing voice synthesis conditioned on a musical score. The proposed method leverages generative models based on stochastic differential equations to achieve singing voice synthesis with increased realism.
content.strength_and_weaknesses: A primary strength of this paper is that the generated singing voice is qualitatively impressive, both to myself and to a panel of human annotators (via MOS scores). The primary weaknesses of this paper are (1) a lack of novelty in the methods, (2) only modest improvements over comparable baselines, and (3) high degrees of "mathiness" detracting from clarity.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity**

This paper suffers from an overwhelming amount of “mathiness”. As far as I can understand from the paper (and please correct me if I’m wrong), the proposed method is a straightforward application of an existing generative model to the task of singing voice synthesis. However, the paper spends around four pages rederiving equations from past work. This is far more than the amount of mathematics that would be necessary to provide helpful background context and notation for explaining how an off-the-shelf method was adapted to an application of interest. Instead, the current presentation may mislead the reader into assuming deeper technical contributions than are actually present in the work. Moreover, the notation is abandoned after section 3.4, suggesting that little of this background information was necessary for outlining / motivating the experiments.

**Quality**

The current description of the experiments leave many details to the imagination. While I appreciate the use of human evaluation as the primary evaluation method, there are many questions unanswered. How many subjects were there? What was their degree of musical expertise? Can we break down the quality further along different axes like musicality, lyrical coherence, and intonation?

This paper also makes some sensational gains regarding the quality of the results. Specifically, the title claims that results are “ultra-realistic”, and the abstract contains that gains over the baselines are “significant”. However, the criteria for “ultra-realism” is never defined, and no statistical test is ever performed to suggest “significant” improvements. Hence, I am forced to make a subjective decision, and to my ears the results sound almost identical to DiffSinger - not really enough to justify something as “ultra-realistic”.

**Novelty**

Unfortunately, there is very little novelty here. The generative modeling approach is an off-the-shelf method, and while impressive, the score-conditioned singing voice synthesis application has been heavily explored (especially recently). I do find it interesting that RealSinger can generate both spectrograms and waveforms end-to-end, but ultimately the complexity of any given method does not feel that important within the context of this application.

**Reproducibility**

It is unlikely that a reader would be able to reproduce the experiments in this paper from the descriptions alone. Are the authors able to release code (as was the case for DiffSinger, a baseline method)?
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the methods presented in this paper do appear to constitute a minor improvement in the competitive landscape of singing-voice synthesis, but unfortunately the paper has a considerable lack of novelty and issues w/ clarity. I would strongly prefer to see a version of this work which focuses much more heavily on the application and multi-faceted evaluation more so than an explanation of the underlying off-the-shelf generative model.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a singing voice synthesis method based on a score-based generative model using stochastic differential equation which was recently acclaimed for high-quality generation. They adapted the existing model to the music audio generation by incorporating the music score encoder and mel spectrogram decoder into the denoising framework. They also extended the singing voice synthesis model to generate raw waveforms in an end-to-end manner. The result show that the propose model outperforms previous work on the same single singer dataset in terms of MOS and mel cepstral distortion. The ablation study reveals some important elements in training the model to improve the quality.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths 
- The quality of synthesized singing voice is very good. When I listened to audio examples in the demo page, the quality of RealSinger was almost not distinguishable from the ground truth. But, I noticed minor hiccup (e.g., instantaneous pitch changes) once or twice in each example. 
- The model comparison and ablation study clearly shows the superiority of the proposed model.
- The related work is comprehensive 

Weaknesses 
- The proposed model is an incremental update based on recent advances in score-based diffusion models. 
- The novel part as an application paper is not much noticeable. The authors should emphasize the novel contribution more clearly.  
- More insightful analysis is necessary to show how the propose model improves the generation quality. 
- The evaluation metric is somewhat simple. MOS could be broken down into more detailed aspects (e.g. pronunciation or naturalness in expression)
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- Clarity

This paper was generally easy to read as long as the reader is familiar with the score-based generative model using stochastic differential equation and related work. The domain-specific part such as lyrics and note/duration encoders requires to read previous work to understand how they are implemented.  

- Quality

The overall writing is acceptable, even though I found some part is hard to catch without reading references.  However, the evaluation part is somewhat weak. They use only one qualitative metric (MOS) and did not specify the number of subjects.  Another issue is that they segmented 127 songs into 5,498 pieces and randomly split them into training, validation and test. This means small pieces from the same song can be used in both training and test? Given that music has many repetitions in melody and lyrics within a song, this experimental setting can be too favorable to the model.  I would suggest to split the dataset song-wise to avoid the problem.   

- Novelty 

This paper presents a high-performance singing voice synthesis model. The main issue is that it is a straightforward application of the recently acclaimed stochastic differential equation model to the singing voice synthesis and the experiment framework was borrowed from the DifferSinger paper.  Although the authors explicitly argue how the proposed model is different from the previous work in page 7, it is not strong enough in view of the ICML standard.

- Reproducibility 

The authors described the proposed model only in a high-level (Section 3.5). They did not specify the model configuration (hyper parameters), the optimizer, and other training details in the experiment. It would be impossible to re-implement the model only with the information in the paper.  


- Minor comments and questions

(title) "Ultra-realistic" in the paper title sounds like an exaggerating term. "Realistic" or "High-quality" would be enough. 

(abstract) What does "ambient Euclidean space" mean in the abstract? "During training, our model learns to accurately predict the direction of movement in the ambient Euclidean space onto the low-dimensional singing voice manifold." 

(page 3) "the FFT model" is used without introducing the full name. 

(page 4, 5) The word "transcribe" is used to mean "synthesize" or "render" in the following sentences. "The decoder will transcribe the music score embedding M S into an approximate corresponding singing voice spectrogram M′" (page 4). "the decoder will transcribe it into the ap- proximated mel-spectrogram M′ (page 5)". But, in generalize, "transcribe" is used to convert audio signals into symbolic sequences (e.g. audio to MIDI in automatic music transcription). 

(page 6) "human-level waveform" --> "natural singing voice waveform" might be a better expression?

(page 6) what is "CHUNK" ? 

(abstract) rectify --> rectifies 
(page 5) show the how RealSinger --> "the" should be removed
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper presents a very impressive singing voice synthesis model with high quality. However, the propose model is a straightforward adaptation of the stochastic differential equation model to the task and the novel contributions are not highly noticeable. Also, the evaluation part is somewhat terse and lacks insightful analysis. I recommend to submit this manuscript to other venues such as Interspeech, ICASSP, or ISMIR after making up for the evaluation part.

content.title: RealSinger: Ultra-Realistic Singing Voice Generation via Stochastic Differential Equations
content.abstract: Synthesizing high-quality singing voice from music score is a challenging problem in music generation and has many practical applications. Samples generated by existing singing voice synthesis (SVS) systems can roughly reflect the lyrics, pitch and duration in a given score, but they fail to contain necessary details. In this paper, based on stochastic differential equations (SDE) we propose RealSinger to generate 22.05kHz ultra-realistic singing voice conditioned on a music score. Our RealSinger learns to find the stochastic process path from a source of white noise to the target singing voice manifold under the conditional music score, allowing to sing the music score while maintaining the local voice details of the target singer. During training, our model learns to accurately predict the direction of movement in the ambient Euclidean space onto the low-dimensional singing voice manifold. RealSinger's framework is very flexible. It can either generate intermediate feature representations of the singing voice, such as mel-spectrogram, or directly generate the final waveform, as in the end-to-end style which rectify defects and accumulation errors introduced by two-stage connected singing synthesis systems. An extensive subjective and objective test on benchmark datasets shows significant gains in perceptual quality using RealSinger. The mean opinion scores (MOS) obtained with RealSinger are closer to those of the human singer's original high-fidelity singing voice than to those obtained with any state-of-the-art method. Audio samples are available at https://realsinger.github.io/.
